terms.def: A brown Triassic sandstone, much of it quarried in Portland, Connecticut, and the dominant rowhouse facing from the 1850s to the 1880s.
terms.spot: Chocolate-brown stone that flakes and spalls with age. Usually a thin veneer over brick, so restorations often use tinted stucco.
ex: Rows in Park Slope, Bedford-Stuyvesant and Harlem

terms.def: A pale, fine-grained sedimentary stone, mostly from Indiana, that carves crisply; the dress of Beaux-Arts and prewar luxury buildings.
terms.spot: Smooth cream or buff stone with sharp carving. Limestone townhouses stand out in brownstone rows from the 1890s on.
ex: 15 Central Park West
Fifth Avenue mansions of the Upper East Side

terms.def: Metamorphic limestone that takes a polish; in New York, much of it white Tuckahoe and Inwood marble.
terms.spot: Brilliant white stone with faint veining; outdoors it weathers to a sugary surface.
ex: Tweed Courthouse, 52 Chambers St
Sun Building (former A.T. Stewart store), 280 Broadway

terms.def: A hard, speckled igneous stone used for bases, steps and heavy structures.
terms.spot: Salt-and-pepper or pink speckles; often the first floor or the stoop, under softer stone.
ex: Towers of the Brooklyn Bridge
Base of the Federal Reserve Bank, 33 Liberty St

terms.def: Brickwork with long sides (stretchers) and short ends (headers) alternating within every course.
terms.spot: Each row goes long-short-long-short, often with darker glazed headers. The giveaway of a Federal house.
ex: Federal houses in the Charlton–King–Vandam Historic District

terms.def: Brickwork showing only long sides, each course offset by half a brick.
terms.spot: No headers at all. Usually means a brick veneer over a steel or concrete frame, so 20th century.
ex: Postwar apartment buildings across the Upper East Side

terms.def: Brickwork with a row of headers every five to seven courses of stretchers. Also called American bond.
terms.spot: Mostly long sides, with a header stripe every sixth row or so; typical of side walls and tenements.
ex: Side walls of 19th-century tenements on the Lower East Side

terms.def: Long, thin brick that stresses horizontal lines, popular around 1890–1915 and again with modernists.
terms.spot: Bricks noticeably flatter and longer than usual, often tan or buff.
ex: Turn-of-the-century townhouses in the Upper East Side Historic District

terms.def: Fired clay molded into ornament or wall cladding, lighter and cheaper than carved stone.
terms.spot: Repeating ornament with crisp identical copies, sometimes glazed to look like stone.
ex: Woolworth Building, 233 Broadway
Bayard–Condict Building, 65 Bleecker St

terms.def: Iron poured into molds, used for prefabricated facades, columns, railings and stoop newels.
terms.spot: Repeated, sharp ornament painted to look like stone; often with rust where the paint chips.
ex: SoHo–Cast Iron Historic District
terms.q: SoHo cast iron building Greene Street

terms.def: Thin galvanized sheet metal stamped into ornament, used for cornices, bay windows and ceilings.
terms.spot: Brownstone cornices are usually this, not stone. Indoors, it's the "tin ceiling".
ex: Cornices on most brownstone rows
Tin ceilings in old storefronts

terms.def: Thin interlocking tiles laid in layers to form self-supporting vaults, patented by Rafael Guastavino in the 1880s.
terms.spot: Herringbone-patterned tile vaults overhead with no visible supports.
ex: Grand Central Oyster Bar, Grand Central Terminal
Former City Hall subway station

terms.def: A blue-gray sandstone split into large flat slabs, used for sidewalks, steps and garden paths.
terms.spot: Big, uneven gray slabs on old sidewalks in front of brownstones.
ex: Sidewalks of Brooklyn Heights and Greenwich Village

terms.def: The green coating copper forms as it weathers outdoors.
terms.spot: Pale green roofs, dormers, cornices and spires.
ex: The Statue of Liberty
Copper dormers and cresting on The Plaza, 768 Fifth Ave

terms.def: Brick with a fired glassy finish that resists dirt; white versions defined postwar "white-brick" buildings.
terms.spot: Shiny brick that reflects light, often white or pale gray.
ex: Manhattan House, 200 East 66th St
